q: What port number does DNS use, which is also the reason behind the name 'Route 53'?

exp.a: Port 80 is used for HTTP traffic, not DNS
exp.b: Port 443 is used for HTTPS traffic, not DNS
exp.c: Correct - DNS uses TCP/UDP Port 53, which is why the service is named Route 53
exp.d: Port 25 is used for SMTP (email), not DNS

q: What are the three main functions of Amazon Route 53?

opts.a: Domain Registration, DNS Routing, Health Checking

exp.a: Correct - Route 53 provides Domain Registration, DNS Routing, and Health Checking as its three core functions
exp.b: Load Balancing and Auto Scaling are ELB and ASG services, not Route 53
exp.c: SSL Termination is handled by ACM/ELB, Caching by CloudFront, not Route 53
exp.d: Firewall and VPN are separate services (WAF, VPN Gateway), not core Route 53 functions

q: What is the availability SLA that AWS provides for Route 53?

exp.a: 99.9% is the SLA for many AWS services, but Route 53 offers higher
exp.b: 99.99% is high but Route 53 offers even higher SLA
exp.c: 99.95% is the SLA for some services like multi-AZ RDS, not Route 53
exp.d: Correct - Route 53 is one of the few AWS services with a 100% availability SLA

q: Which DNS record type maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?

exp.a: AAAA record maps to IPv6 addresses, not IPv4
exp.b: CNAME maps a domain to another domain name, not directly to an IP
exp.c: Correct - A record maps a domain name directly to an IPv4 address
exp.d: MX record is used for mail exchange routing, not IP mapping

q: Which DNS record type is specific to Route 53 and can be used at the zone apex?

exp.a: CNAME CANNOT be used at the zone apex - this is a DNS specification limitation
exp.b: Correct - Alias is a Route 53-specific record that works at zone apex and points to AWS resources for free
exp.c: NS records are standard DNS records for name server delegation, not Route 53-specific
exp.d: PTR is a standard reverse DNS lookup record, not Route 53-specific

q: How many name servers does Route 53 assign to each hosted zone?

exp.a: Route 53 assigns more than 2 name servers for redundancy
exp.b: Route 53 assigns more than 3 name servers
exp.c: Correct - Route 53 assigns 4 name servers across different TLDs (.com, .net, .org, .co.uk) for each hosted zone
exp.d: Route 53 assigns exactly 4, not 5 name servers

q: What is the default health check interval in Route 53?

exp.a: 10 seconds is the 'fast' interval option which costs more
exp.b: Correct - The default (standard) health check interval is 30 seconds
exp.c: 60 seconds is not a Route 53 health check interval option
exp.d: 5 seconds is not a Route 53 health check interval option

q: How many global health checkers does Route 53 use to monitor an endpoint?

exp.a: Route 53 uses more than 5 health checkers for reliability
exp.b: Route 53 uses more than 10 health checkers
exp.c: Correct - Route 53 uses 15 global health checkers distributed across multiple regions
exp.d: Route 53 uses exactly 15, not 20 health checkers

q: What percentage of Route 53 health checkers must report healthy for an endpoint to be considered healthy?

exp.a: 50% is too high - Route 53 uses a lower threshold
exp.b: 30% is not the correct threshold
exp.c: Correct - At least 18% of health checkers (approximately 3 out of 15) must report healthy
exp.d: 25% is not the correct Route 53 health check threshold

q: What is the cost of Alias record DNS queries to AWS resources in Route 53?

exp.a: $0.40 per million is the cost for standard (non-Alias) queries
exp.b: $0.60 per million is the cost for latency-based queries
exp.c: $0.50 per million is not the correct pricing tier
exp.d: Correct - Alias queries to AWS resources (ELB, CloudFront, S3, etc.) are completely FREE

q: What is the monthly cost of a hosted zone in Route 53?

exp.a: $0.25 is not the correct hosted zone pricing
exp.b: Correct - Each hosted zone costs $0.50 per month
exp.c: $1.00 is not the correct hosted zone pricing
exp.d: $0.75 is not the correct hosted zone pricing

q: Which two VPC settings must be enabled for a Route 53 private hosted zone to work?

opts.b: DNS Hostnames and VPC Flow Logs

exp.a: Correct - Both enableDnsHostnames and enableDnsSupport must be set to true in the VPC
exp.b: VPC Flow Logs are for network monitoring, not DNS resolution
exp.c: NAT Gateway is for internet access from private subnets, not related to private DNS
exp.d: Internet Gateway provides internet access, not required for private DNS resolution

q: How many routing policies does Route 53 support?

exp.a: Route 53 supports more than 5 routing policies
exp.b: Route 53 supports more than 6 routing policies
exp.c: Route 53 had 7 originally but IP-based routing was added
exp.d: Correct - 8 routing policies: Simple, Weighted, Latency, Failover, Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multi-Value Answer, and IP-based

q: Which routing policy does NOT support health checks?

exp.a: Weighted routing DOES support health checks
exp.b: Correct - Simple routing does NOT support health checks. If multiple values are returned, the client chooses randomly
exp.c: Latency-based routing DOES support health checks
exp.d: Failover routing requires health checks on the primary record (mandatory)

q: What is the maximum number of records Route 53 Multi-Value Answer routing can return per query?

exp.a: Multi-Value can return more than 4 records
exp.b: Multi-Value can return more than 6 records
exp.c: Correct - Multi-Value Answer routing returns up to 8 healthy records per DNS query
exp.d: The maximum is 8, not 10 records per query

q: A company has a web application deployed in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. They want users to be routed to the region with the fastest response time. If one region is unhealthy, traffic should automatically route to the healthy region. Which configuration should they use?

opts.a: Weighted routing policy with health checks
opts.b: Geolocation routing policy with health checks
opts.c: Latency-based routing policy with health checks
opts.d: Simple routing policy with multiple values

exp.a: Weighted routing distributes by percentage, doesn't consider actual latency/speed
exp.b: Geolocation routes based on user's location, not fastest response time
exp.c: Correct - Latency-based routing measures network latency to AWS regions and routes to the fastest. Health checks enable automatic failover
exp.d: Simple routing doesn't support health checks and returns random values

q: A company needs to point their zone apex (example.com) to an Application Load Balancer. Which record type should they create?

opts.a: CNAME record pointing to the ALB DNS name
opts.b: A record with Alias pointing to the ALB
opts.c: A record with the ALB's IP address
opts.d: NS record pointing to the ALB

exp.a: CNAME CANNOT be used at the zone apex (naked domain) - this is a DNS specification rule (RFC)
exp.b: Correct - Alias A record works at zone apex, points to ALB, is free, and automatically tracks ALB IP changes
exp.c: ALB does not have a static IP address - IPs change dynamically, so hardcoding won't work
exp.d: NS records are for delegating DNS authority to name servers, not for routing traffic to ALBs

q: A company hosts a static website on S3 at domain 'blog.example.com'. They created an S3 bucket named 'my-blog-bucket' and an Alias record in Route 53. The setup is not working. What is the issue?

opts.a: S3 static websites don't support Alias records
opts.b: The bucket name must be 'blog.example.com' to match the domain
opts.c: They need to use CNAME instead of Alias
opts.d: They need to enable CORS on the bucket

exp.a: S3 website endpoints ARE valid Alias targets in Route 53
exp.b: Correct - For Route 53 Alias to S3 website endpoint, the bucket name MUST exactly match the domain/subdomain name
exp.c: Alias is the preferred choice (free queries, works at apex). CNAME works for subdomains but Alias is better
exp.d: CORS is for cross-origin browser requests, not DNS resolution issues

q: A company wants to monitor the health of an RDS instance in a private subnet using Route 53 health checks. What is the recommended approach?

opts.a: Create a health check pointing to the RDS private IP
opts.b: Create a VPC endpoint for Route 53 health checkers
opts.c: Create a CloudWatch alarm for RDS, then create a Route 53 health check based on the alarm
opts.d: Move the RDS instance to a public subnet

exp.a: Route 53 health checkers are outside the VPC and cannot reach private IP addresses
exp.b: No VPC endpoint exists for Route 53 health checkers
exp.c: Correct - For private resources, use CloudWatch Metric → CloudWatch Alarm → Route 53 Health Check as a bridge
exp.d: Moving RDS to a public subnet is a terrible security practice and unnecessary

q: A company registered their domain with GoDaddy but wants to use Route 53 as their DNS service. What should they do?

opts.a: Create a Private Hosted Zone in Route 53 and copy NS records to GoDaddy
opts.b: Create a Public Hosted Zone in Route 53 and update NS records at GoDaddy with Route 53's name servers
opts.c: Transfer the domain to Route 53 first, then create a hosted zone
opts.d: Create an Alias record in Route 53 pointing to GoDaddy's DNS

exp.a: Private Hosted Zone is for internal VPC resolution only, not public internet DNS
exp.b: Correct - Create a Public Hosted Zone (Route 53 gives 4 NS records), then update NS records at registrar to Route 53's name servers
exp.c: Domain transfer is NOT required to use Route 53 as DNS service - you can separate registrar and DNS
exp.d: Alias records point TO AWS resources, not to external DNS providers

q: Route 53 health checks are reporting unhealthy for a web server even though users can access it normally. What is the most likely cause?

opts.a: The health check TTL is too high
opts.b: The security group is not allowing inbound traffic from Route 53 health checker IP ranges
opts.c: The health check interval is set to 30 seconds
opts.d: Route 53 health checks only work with ELB

exp.a: TTL affects caching duration, not health check pass/fail results
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 health checkers send requests from public IPs. If security groups don't allow these IPs, checks always fail even though users (from different IPs) can access normally
exp.c: 30-second interval is the default and doesn't cause false unhealthy results
exp.d: Health checks work with any endpoint - EC2, ALB, on-premises servers, etc.

q: A company uses Failover routing. After primary fails, it takes 5 minutes for traffic to reach secondary. How can they reduce failover time?

opts.a: Increase the number of health checker regions
opts.b: Change health check interval to 10 seconds (fast) and reduce failure threshold
opts.c: Reduce the TTL on the Alias record
opts.d: Add a second health check on the secondary record

exp.a: Adding more regions doesn't speed up detection - threshold is percentage-based (18%)
exp.b: Correct - Fast interval (10s vs 30s) + lower failure threshold (1-2 vs 3) dramatically reduces detection time from ~90s to ~10-20s
exp.c: Alias records have TTL automatically managed by Route 53 - you cannot manually change it
exp.d: Secondary health check doesn't affect how fast the primary failure is detected

q: A company has 50 microservices in a VPC needing internal DNS names like 'payment.internal' that should NOT be resolvable from the internet. What should they use?

opts.a: Public hosted zone with security group restrictions
opts.b: Private hosted zone associated with the VPC
opts.d: CNAME records in a public hosted zone

exp.a: Public hosted zones are always resolvable from the internet - security groups don't protect DNS queries
exp.b: Correct - Private hosted zone provides DNS resolution only within associated VPCs, not accessible from internet
exp.c: Resolver inbound endpoints are for on-premises to AWS DNS resolution, not internal service discovery
exp.d: Records in public hosted zones are publicly queryable regardless of the target's accessibility

q: On-premises applications need to resolve AWS private hosted zone records. The environments are connected via Direct Connect. Which Route 53 Resolver component is needed?

exp.a: Outbound Endpoint is for AWS → on-premises direction (opposite of what's needed)
exp.b: Correct - Inbound Endpoint allows on-premises DNS servers to forward queries INTO Route 53 for resolution
exp.c: Resolver Rules are used with Outbound Endpoints to define which domains to forward to on-premises
exp.d: DNS Firewall filters outbound VPC DNS queries, doesn't handle inbound from on-premises

q: A company uses Weighted routing with Record A (weight=70), Record B (weight=20), Record C (weight=10). They set Record C weight to 0. What happens?

opts.b: Record C gets no traffic; A gets ~78% and B gets ~22%

exp.a: Equal traffic only happens when ALL records have weight = 0
exp.b: Correct - Weight 0 means no traffic. Remaining: A = 70/(70+20) ≈ 78%, B = 20/(70+20) ≈ 22%
exp.c: Traffic continues flowing to records with non-zero weights
exp.d: Weight = 0 explicitly means NO traffic is sent to that record

q: What is the monthly cost of a Route 53 Traffic Flow Policy Record?

exp.a: $10/month is not the correct Traffic Flow pricing
exp.b: $25/month is not the correct Traffic Flow pricing
exp.c: Correct - Each Traffic Flow Policy Record costs $50/month
exp.d: $100/month is not the correct Traffic Flow pricing

q: Which Route 53 routing policy REQUIRES Route 53 Traffic Flow to function?

exp.a: Geolocation routing works without Traffic Flow
exp.b: Latency-based routing works without Traffic Flow
exp.c: Correct - Geoproximity routing with bias values REQUIRES Route 53 Traffic Flow and its visual editor
exp.d: Multi-Value Answer routing works without Traffic Flow

q: A company configures Route 53 DNS Firewall with: Rule 1 (Priority 100): BLOCK malware-list, Rule 2 (Priority 200): ALERT suspicious-list, Rule 3 (Priority 300): ALLOW all. A query matches BOTH malware-list and suspicious-list. What happens?

opts.a: Query is allowed because ALLOW rule exists
opts.b: Query triggers ALERT and is allowed
opts.d: Query is both blocked and alerted

exp.a: ALLOW rule at Priority 300 is never reached because a lower priority rule matches first
exp.b: ALERT rule at Priority 200 is never reached because Rule 1 (Priority 100) matches first
exp.c: Correct - Rules evaluated in priority order (lowest number = highest priority). Rule 1 matches first → BLOCKED. Evaluation stops
exp.d: Only ONE action is taken per query - first matching rule wins, evaluation stops immediately

q: What is the default maximum number of hosted zones per AWS account in Route 53?

exp.a: 100 is the limit for reusable delegation sets, not hosted zones
exp.b: 200 is the default limit for health checks per account, not hosted zones
exp.c: Correct - Default limit is 500 hosted zones per account (soft limit, can be increased)
exp.d: 1000 is the limit for resolver rules per region, not hosted zones

q: What is the default maximum number of records per hosted zone in Route 53?

exp.a: 1,000 is too low - Route 53 supports more records per zone
exp.b: 5,000 is not the correct limit
exp.c: Correct - Default limit is 10,000 records per hosted zone (soft limit, can be increased)
exp.d: 50,000 exceeds the default limit

q: How many bytes of the response body does Route 53 health check string matching inspect?

exp.a: 1,024 bytes is too small - Route 53 checks more
exp.b: 2,048 bytes is not the correct value
exp.c: Correct - Route 53 health checks with string matching inspect the first 5,120 bytes of the response body
exp.d: 10,240 bytes exceeds what Route 53 inspects

q: What is the maximum number of child health checks that can be combined in a Route 53 Calculated Health Check?

exp.a: 10 is too low - Calculated Health Checks support many more children
exp.b: 50 is not the correct limit
exp.c: 128 is not the correct limit
exp.d: Correct - A Calculated Health Check can monitor up to 256 child health checks

q: A company needs an ACM certificate for a CloudFront distribution serving 'www.example.com'. In which region must the certificate be created?

opts.a: The region closest to most users
opts.c: Any region - ACM certificates are global
opts.d: The region where Route 53 hosted zone exists

exp.a: User proximity doesn't determine ACM certificate region for CloudFront
exp.b: Correct - ACM certificates for CloudFront (and Edge-Optimized API Gateway) MUST be in us-east-1
exp.c: ACM certificates are regional, NOT global. CloudFront specifically requires us-east-1
exp.d: Route 53 is a global service without a specific region - this doesn't affect ACM placement

q: A company needs an ACM certificate for a Regional API Gateway in eu-west-1. In which region must the certificate be created?

exp.a: us-east-1 is required for CloudFront/Edge-Optimized API GW, NOT Regional API Gateway
exp.b: Correct - Regional API Gateway requires the ACM certificate in the SAME region (eu-west-1)
exp.c: ACM certificates are regional and must be in the correct region for the service using them
exp.d: Only one certificate is needed, in the same region as the Regional API Gateway

q: What HTTP status codes does Route 53 health check consider as healthy?

exp.a: Route 53 accepts more than just 200 status code
exp.b: Correct - Route 53 health checks consider any 2xx or 3xx HTTP status code as healthy
exp.c: 3xx (redirects) are also considered healthy, not just 2xx
exp.d: 4xx (client errors like 404, 403) are NOT considered healthy

q: A company uses Route 53 Failover routing with health checks. The primary is healthy but users report being routed to the secondary (maintenance page). What is the most likely cause?

opts.a: The secondary health check is failing
opts.b: The primary health check is misconfigured and reporting unhealthy to Route 53
opts.c: Failover routing doesn't support S3 as secondary
opts.d: The TTL on the primary record is set to 0

exp.a: Secondary health check failure wouldn't cause traffic to route TO the secondary
exp.b: Correct - If Route 53 routes to secondary, it believes primary is unhealthy. The health check is likely misconfigured (wrong endpoint, port, path, or security group blocking health checker IPs)
exp.c: S3 is a perfectly valid and common secondary target for maintenance pages
exp.d: TTL of 0 affects caching duration, not the routing decision itself

q: A company wants GDPR compliance (EU users must ALWAYS go to EU servers) AND best performance within allowed regions. Which combination of routing policies with Traffic Flow should they use?

opts.b: Geolocation for EU → eu-west-1, Latency-based for other regions via Traffic Flow
opts.c: Geoproximity with positive bias on EU region
opts.d: Weighted routing with 100% to EU for European users

exp.a: Latency alone cannot GUARANTEE EU users stay in EU - they might get routed to US if latency is lower
exp.b: Correct - Geolocation provides STRICT geographic boundary (compliance), Latency-based optimizes performance within allowed regions. Traffic Flow enables combining policies
exp.c: Geoproximity doesn't provide strict boundaries - bias can be overridden by distance calculations
exp.d: Weighted routing doesn't route based on user geographic location

q: A company has a Route 53 private hosted zone in Account A. Account B's VPC needs to resolve these records. The architect cannot find the cross-account option in the console. What is correct?

opts.a: Share the hosted zone via AWS RAM
opts.b: Use CLI: create-vpc-association-authorization in Account A, then associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone in Account B
opts.c: Create VPC peering between accounts first
opts.d: Create a duplicate hosted zone in Account B

exp.a: Hosted zones CANNOT be shared via RAM - only Resolver Rules, DNS Firewall Rules, and Profiles can
exp.b: Correct - Cross-account private hosted zone association is CLI/API only. Three steps: authorize in Account A, associate in Account B, delete authorization (cleanup)
exp.c: VPC peering provides network connectivity but doesn't enable cross-account DNS resolution
exp.d: Duplicating defeats centralized management and records would need manual synchronization

q: A company plans a DNS migration next week. Current TTL is 86400 seconds (24 hours). They need changes to propagate within 60 seconds during migration. What is the correct strategy?

opts.a: Lower TTL to 60 seconds and immediately make the change
opts.b: Lower TTL to 60 seconds NOW, wait 24 hours for old caches to expire, then make the change next week
opts.c: Delete the old record and create a new one with 60-second TTL
opts.d: Contact AWS support to flush DNS caches globally

exp.a: Lowering TTL immediately doesn't flush existing caches - resolvers still hold the old 24-hour cached response
exp.b: Correct - Must lower TTL first, then wait for the OLD TTL duration (24 hours) for all caches to expire. After that, changes propagate within the new 60-second TTL
exp.c: Deleting/recreating doesn't help - external resolvers still have the old response cached for 24 hours
exp.d: AWS cannot control external DNS resolver caches worldwide

q: A company uses Route 53 DNSSEC. Which CloudWatch alarm metrics should they monitor for DNSSEC issues?

exp.a: These are not valid Route 53 DNSSEC CloudWatch metrics
exp.b: Correct - Monitor DNSSECInternalFailure (internal signing issues) and DNSSECKeySigningKeysNeedingAction (KSK needs attention/rotation)
exp.c: These are not valid Route 53 DNSSEC CloudWatch metrics
exp.d: These are health check metrics, not DNSSEC-specific metrics

q: EC2 instances are exfiltrating data via DNS tunneling. The security team wants to block queries to malicious domains. They also want 'fail-close' behavior if the firewall itself fails. Which configuration is correct?

opts.b: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with BLOCK rules and fail-close configuration
opts.c: AWS WAF with DNS inspection rules
opts.d: Network ACL blocking all DNS traffic

exp.a: Security groups can't inspect domain names within DNS queries - only IP/port level filtering
exp.b: Correct - DNS Firewall blocks specific malicious domains. Fail-close means if firewall fails, ALL queries are blocked (security over availability)
exp.c: AWS WAF inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic, not DNS queries
exp.d: Blocking ALL DNS would break all applications - need selective domain-level blocking

q: A company has Multi-Value Answer routing with 12 records and health checks. 4 are unhealthy. If ALL 12 records become unhealthy, what does Route 53 return?

opts.b: Returns all 12 records regardless of health (best effort)
opts.c: Returns the last known 8 healthy records from cache
opts.d: Returns an error to the client

exp.a: Route 53 doesn't return empty response when all are unhealthy
exp.b: Correct - When ALL records are unhealthy, Route 53 returns all records anyway as a best-effort mechanism (better than returning nothing)
exp.c: Route 53 doesn't cache previous healthy states for Multi-Value responses
exp.d: Route 53 doesn't return errors - it always provides a DNS response

q: A company shares Route 53 Resolver Rules across 20 accounts via AWS RAM. Which resources CAN be shared via RAM for Route 53?

opts.a: Hosted Zones, Resolver Rules, Health Checks
opts.b: Resolver Rules, DNS Firewall Rule Groups, Route 53 Profiles
opts.c: Hosted Zones, DNS Firewall Rule Groups, Resolver Endpoints
opts.d: Resolver Rules, Resolver Endpoints, Health Checks

exp.a: Hosted Zones and Health Checks CANNOT be shared via RAM
exp.b: Correct - Only Resolver Rules, DNS Firewall Rule Groups, and Route 53 Profiles can be shared via AWS RAM
exp.c: Hosted Zones and Resolver Endpoints cannot be shared via RAM
exp.d: Resolver Endpoints and Health Checks cannot be shared via RAM

q: A company uses Route 53 with Geoproximity routing. Resources are in us-east-1 (bias=0) and eu-west-1 (bias=0). They want to shift traffic from US to EU gradually. What should they do?

exp.a: Positive bias EXPANDS the region - increasing US bias would attract MORE traffic to US (opposite effect)
exp.b: Correct - Positive bias on eu-west-1 EXPANDS its geographic region, pulling more users toward EU and away from US
exp.c: Negative bias SHRINKS the region - this would push traffic AWAY from EU (opposite effect)
exp.d: Weighted routing works but doesn't use geographic proximity and is a different approach entirely

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid Alias record target in Route 53?

exp.a: ALB IS a valid Alias target
exp.b: Correct - EC2 instance DNS name is NOT a valid Alias target. EC2 DNS names are ephemeral and change on stop/start. Use regular A record with Elastic IP or put EC2 behind an ELB
exp.c: CloudFront distribution IS a valid Alias target
exp.d: S3 website endpoint IS a valid Alias target (bucket name must match domain)

q: A company uses Route 53 with ACM DNS validation. They clicked 'Create record in Route 53' but the certificate stays in 'Pending validation' for over 24 hours. What is the most likely cause?

opts.a: The ACM certificate is in the wrong region
opts.b: The domain's NS records at the registrar point to a different DNS provider, not Route 53
opts.c: DNS validation only works with private hosted zones
opts.d: The CNAME validation record TTL is too high

exp.a: ACM region affects which service can use it, not the validation process itself
exp.b: Correct - ACM validates by querying PUBLIC DNS. If NS records point elsewhere, the CNAME was created in Route 53 but ACM queries the other provider where the record doesn't exist
exp.c: DNS validation requires PUBLIC DNS resolution - works with public hosted zones
exp.d: TTL doesn't prevent ACM from finding the validation CNAME record

q: A Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoint needs to be highly available. What is the minimum configuration required?

exp.a: Single ENI in 1 AZ is not highly available - single point of failure
exp.b: Correct - Minimum 2 ENIs across 2 different AZs for high availability. Each IP handles 10,000 queries/second
exp.c: 3 ENIs is more than minimum required, though possible for extra capacity
exp.d: 4 ENIs is more than minimum required for HA

q: What is the maximum number of queries per second each Route 53 Resolver Endpoint IP can handle?

exp.a: 1,000 queries/second is too low for a Resolver Endpoint IP
exp.b: 5,000 queries/second is not the correct capacity
exp.c: Correct - Each Resolver Endpoint IP can handle 10,000 DNS queries per second
exp.d: 50,000 exceeds the per-IP capacity of a Resolver Endpoint

q: A company implements Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC). They want to prevent an operator from accidentally turning off ALL routing controls (causing total outage). Which ARC component prevents this?

exp.a: Readiness Checks verify DR resources are configured properly, don't prevent operator mistakes
exp.b: Routing Controls are the on/off switches themselves - they don't prevent misuse
exp.c: Correct - Safety Rules (specifically Assertion Rules) enforce that at least N routing controls must remain ON, preventing accidental total outage
exp.d: Cluster endpoints provide HA for the control plane, don't enforce operational guardrails

q: A company uses Split-View DNS with the same domain 'app.example.com' in both public and private hosted zones. An EC2 instance in the associated VPC queries this domain. Which hosted zone responds?

opts.a: Public hosted zone (public always takes priority)
opts.b: Private hosted zone (private takes priority for VPC queries)
opts.c: Both respond and client picks one
opts.d: Whichever has lower TTL responds first

exp.a: Public hosted zone does NOT take priority for queries from within the VPC
exp.b: Correct - For queries originating WITHIN an associated VPC, the Private Hosted Zone ALWAYS takes priority over the Public Hosted Zone
exp.c: Only one hosted zone responds per query - Route 53 doesn't return both
exp.d: TTL doesn't determine which hosted zone is queried

q: A company wants to log ALL DNS queries made by VPC resources and send them to S3 for long-term analysis. Which feature should they use?

opts.a: Route 53 DNS Query Logging (to CloudWatch Logs in us-east-1)
opts.c: VPC Flow Logs filtering on port 53

exp.a: DNS Query Logging is for PUBLIC hosted zone queries only and only supports CloudWatch Logs destination
exp.b: Correct - Resolver Query Logging captures ALL VPC DNS queries and supports CloudWatch Logs, S3, OR Kinesis Data Firehose as destinations
exp.c: VPC Flow Logs capture IP/port metadata but cannot show domain names being queried
exp.d: CloudTrail logs Route 53 API management calls, not DNS resolution queries

q: Route 53 DNS Query Logging for public hosted zones can ONLY send logs to which destination and in which region?

opts.c: Kinesis Data Firehose in the same region as hosted zone

exp.a: DNS Query Logging does not support S3 as a destination (Resolver Query Logging does)
exp.b: Correct - DNS Query Logging for public hosted zones sends logs ONLY to CloudWatch Logs and the log group MUST be in us-east-1
exp.c: DNS Query Logging does not support Kinesis Data Firehose (Resolver Query Logging does)
exp.d: The CloudWatch Logs log group must specifically be in us-east-1, not any region

q: A company uses Route 53 Geolocation routing. They configured records for Europe and United States but forgot to create a Default record. A user from Australia makes a DNS query. What happens?

opts.a: Route 53 returns the geographically closest record (Europe or US)
opts.b: Route 53 returns no answer (NXDOMAIN or empty response)
opts.c: Route 53 randomly picks between Europe and US records
opts.d: Route 53 returns all records and client picks one

exp.a: Geolocation doesn't fall back to nearest location - it's strict matching only
exp.b: Correct - Without a Default record, users from non-matching locations receive NO answer. This is why creating a Default record is CRITICAL
exp.c: Route 53 doesn't randomly assign geolocation records
exp.d: Geolocation returns only the matching record, not all records

q: What is the Geolocation routing resolution priority when multiple records could match?

exp.a: This is reversed - most specific wins, not least specific
exp.b: Default has the lowest priority, not highest
exp.c: Correct - Most specific wins: US State > Country > Continent > Default. A user in California matches State first, then Country (US), then Continent (North America), then Default
exp.d: State is more specific than Country and should be evaluated first

q: A company uses Route 53 Calculated Health Check with 5 children. They set minimum healthy = 3. When does the parent report UNHEALTHY?

opts.a: When 1 or more children are unhealthy
opts.b: When 2 or more children are unhealthy
opts.c: When 3 or more children are unhealthy

exp.a: With minimum 3 healthy, 1 unhealthy still leaves 4 healthy (above threshold)
exp.b: With minimum 3 healthy, 2 unhealthy still leaves 3 healthy (meets threshold exactly)
exp.c: Correct - Minimum healthy = 3 means parent needs at least 3 healthy children. If 3+ are unhealthy, only 2 or fewer are healthy → parent = UNHEALTHY
exp.d: The parent becomes unhealthy before all 5 fail - it triggers when fewer than 3 are healthy

q: How are Route 53 Reusable Delegation Sets created?

opts.a: Through the AWS Console under Route 53 settings
opts.b: Through AWS CLI/API only - not available in the Console
opts.c: Automatically created when you register a domain

exp.a: Reusable Delegation Sets are NOT available in the AWS Console
exp.b: Correct - Reusable Delegation Sets can ONLY be created via CLI or API (aws route53 create-reusable-delegation-set)
exp.c: Domain registration creates a regular delegation set, not a reusable one
exp.d: They can be created via CLI/API directly, CloudFormation is not the only method

q: What is the maximum number of VPCs that can be associated with a single Route 53 private hosted zone?

exp.a: 5 is far too low - many more VPCs can be associated
exp.b: 100 is not the correct limit
exp.c: Correct - Up to 300 VPCs can be associated with a single private hosted zone
exp.d: 500 is the limit for hosted zones per account, not VPCs per hosted zone

q: A company configures Route 53 DNS Firewall with 'fail-open' behavior. What happens if the DNS Firewall service itself experiences a failure?

opts.a: All DNS queries are blocked until firewall recovers
opts.b: All DNS queries are allowed through without filtering
opts.c: DNS queries are queued until firewall recovers
opts.d: DNS queries are routed to an alternate firewall

exp.a: This describes 'fail-close' behavior, not 'fail-open'
exp.b: Correct - Fail-open means if the firewall fails, all queries are ALLOWED through (availability prioritized over security)
exp.c: DNS queries are not queued - they need immediate resolution
exp.d: There's no alternate firewall routing - it's either fail-open or fail-close

q: A company has a Calculated Health Check (parent) with 5 children. They want the parent to be UNHEALTHY only when ALL children are unhealthy. How should they configure it?

exp.a: Minimum 5 means ALL must be healthy - parent goes unhealthy if even 1 child fails (too strict)
exp.b: Correct - Minimum healthy = 1 means parent stays HEALTHY as long as at least 1 child is healthy. Only when ALL 5 fail (0 healthy) does parent become UNHEALTHY
exp.c: The logic type (AND/OR) is separate from numeric threshold - and minimum 5 is too strict
exp.d: Minimum 0 would mean parent is always healthy regardless of children (defeats purpose)

q: What is the Geoproximity bias range in Route 53?

exp.a: -100 and +100 are outside the valid range
exp.b: Correct - Geoproximity bias ranges from -99 (shrink region) to +99 (expand region), with 0 being neutral
exp.c: -50 to +50 is too narrow - the actual range extends to ±99
exp.d: -999 to +999 is far too large - the range is limited to ±99

q: A company wants to use Route 53 for both public internet users AND internal VPC users with the same domain name but different IP addresses. What is this pattern called?

exp.a: DNS Forwarding is sending queries to another DNS server, not serving different answers for same domain
exp.b: Correct - Split-View/Split-Horizon DNS uses same domain name with both Public and Private Hosted Zones, returning different answers based on query origin
exp.c: DNS Delegation is assigning subdomains to different name servers, not serving different answers
exp.d: Hybrid DNS refers to on-premises + cloud DNS integration, not same-domain different-answer pattern

q: How many IPs can a single Route 53 Resolver Endpoint have (maximum)?

exp.a: 2 is the minimum for HA, not the maximum
exp.b: 4 is the limit for resolver endpoints per region per direction, not IPs per endpoint
exp.c: Correct - Each Resolver Endpoint can have a maximum of 6 IP addresses (ENIs)
exp.d: 8 exceeds the maximum IPs per endpoint

q: A company has Route 53 with Weighted routing. ALL three records have weight set to 0. What happens to traffic?

opts.a: All traffic stops - no responses returned
opts.b: Traffic is distributed equally among all three records
opts.d: Only the first record receives traffic

exp.a: Route 53 doesn't stop traffic when all weights are 0 - it has special behavior
exp.b: Correct - When ALL records have weight = 0, Route 53 distributes traffic EQUALLY among all records (special case)
exp.c: Route 53 doesn't return errors for this configuration
exp.d: Traffic goes to all records equally, not just the first one
